scenes.title: Summary

educational.emphasis: Visualizing the squares on the sides helps understand why the formula involves squaring the lengths.

test_case.description: 泰勒公式：如何用多项式逼近任意光滑函数

visuals: Static function f(x) vs. Taylor polynomial P_n(x) graph
logic_steps: Start with a known point a on the function
Match the function value (0th derivative)
Match the slope (1st derivative)
Match the curvature/concavity (2nd derivative)
Generalize to the nth derivative

scenes.title: Introduction to Approximation
scenes.description: Introduce the problem: Complex functions (like sin(x)) are hard to calculate by hand. We need a way to approximate them using simpler polynomials.
visual_elements: Icon of a calculator vs. a polynomial equation

scenes.title: The Logic of Matching Derivatives
scenes.description: Explain the core concept: To make a polynomial look like a function at point x=a, they must share the same position, slope, and curvature.
visual_elements: Animation of a line approaching a curve to match slope
Visual highlighting of f(a), f'(a), f''(a)

scenes.title: Constructing the Formula
scenes.description: Derive the formula step-by-step. Show how dividing by n! accounts for the power rule differentiation.
visual_elements: Animation showing (x-a)^n becoming n! after n differentiations

scenes.title: Visualizing Convergence
scenes.description: Demonstrate the Taylor series for e^x or sin(x). Show how adding more terms (n=0, 1, 2, 5...) makes the polynomial fit the curve better over a wider range.

scenes.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
scenes.description: Recap the formula and the concept of local approximation turning into global representation.

key_points: Taylor series turns calculus into algebra
It uses local information (derivatives at a) to predict global behavior
Higher degree = Better accuracy (usually)
educational.emphasis: Focus on the geometric meaning of derivatives (slope, curve, wiggle) rather than just algebraic manipulation.

scenes.title: The Power of Polynomials
scenes.description: Introduce the challenge: complex functions (sin, exp) are hard to calculate, but polynomials are easy. Show the goal: approximating a smooth curve with a polynomial.

scenes.title: Step 1: Matching Position (0th Order)
scenes.description: Start with the simplest approximation: a constant. Ensure the polynomial passes through the point (a, f(a)).

scenes.title: Step 2: Matching Slope (1st Order)
scenes.description: Improve the fit by adding the linear term. Make the tangent line of the polynomial match the derivative of the function.
visual_elements: Tangent line animation at point a
Visual comparison of flat line vs tangent line

scenes.title: Step 3: Matching Curvature (2nd Order & Beyond)
scenes.description: Add the quadratic term to match the concavity (second derivative). Show how adding higher-order terms (n=3, 4...) forces the polynomial to hug the curve tighter.

scenes.title: The General Formula & Summary
scenes.description: Reveal the full Taylor Series formula. Summarize the logic: we are matching derivatives of all orders to create a 'local' copy of the function.

visualization.primary_visual: Split screen or overlay showing the target function (e.g., sine wave) and the Taylor polynomial curve evolving order by order (n=0 to n=5).

key_points: Any smooth function can be approximated by a polynomial near a specific point.
The 'Order' of the polynomial determines how accurate the approximation is.
The coefficients are determined by the function's derivatives at the center point.
Higher derivatives correspond to more subtle geometric properties (curvature, rate of change of curvature).
educational.emphasis: Visual intuition of 'hugging the curve' by matching geometric properties (value, slope, bend).

scenes.title: Introduction to Quadratic Equations
scenes.description: Display the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0. Show a parabola intersecting the x-axis to visualize roots.

scenes.title: Completing the Square
scenes.description: Step-by-step algebraic manipulation: divide by a, move constant term, add (b/2a)² to both sides.

scenes.title: Deriving the Formula
scenes.description: Factor the perfect square, take the square root, and solve for x to arrive at the quadratic formula.
visual_elements: Transition from completed square to root formula

scenes.title: Geometric Interpretation
scenes.description: Explain the geometry: -b/2a is the axis of symmetry (vertex x-coordinate), and the square root term represents the distance from the vertex to the roots.

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Recap the final formula and the core concept of completing the square.

key_points: Completing the square is the bridge between the standard form and the root formula.
The term -b/2a locates the vertex (axis of symmetry).
The discriminant (b² - 4ac) determines the number of real roots.
educational.emphasis: Visualizing the algebraic steps as geometric transformations helps in understanding why the formula works, rather than just memorizing it.

logic_steps: Define the Mean (μ) as the center and peak of the distribution
Define Standard Deviation (σ) as the measure of spread/width
Demonstrate that 68% of data falls within 1σ of the mean
Demonstrate that 95% of data falls within 2σ of the mean
Demonstrate that 99.7% of data falls within 3σ of the mean

scenes.title: Introduction to the Bell Curve
scenes.description: Visual introduction of the Normal Distribution curve. Show its symmetrical 'bell' shape and identify the highest point as the Mean (μ).
visual_elements: Static or slowly drawing Bell Curve
Label for Mean (μ) at the center

scenes.title: Understanding Standard Deviation
scenes.description: Explain Standard Deviation (σ) visually. Show how the curve changes shape (becomes flatter or steeper) as σ changes, but the area remains 1. Mark the 1σ, 2σ, and 3σ distances from the mean.
visual_elements: Animation of curve widening and narrowing
Vertical lines appearing at μ±1σ, μ±2σ, μ±3σ

scenes.title: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
scenes.description: Step-by-step shading of areas under the curve. First shade the center (μ±1σ) and label '68%'. Then expand to (μ±2σ) and label '95%'. Finally expand to (μ±3σ) and label '99.7%'.
visual_elements: Color-coded regions (e.g., light blue for 1σ, darker for 2σ)

scenes.title: Real-World Example
scenes.description: Apply the rule to a concrete example, such as Human Height or Test Scores. If the average is 170cm and σ is 10cm, show that 68% of people are between 160cm and 180cm.
visual_elements: Icons or text representing the specific example (e.g., 'Height: 170cm')

scenes.title: Summary
scenes.description: Recap the main points: Symmetry, Mean = Center, and the Empirical Rule percentages.
visual_elements: Final clean view of the curve with all labels

key_points: The curve is symmetrical around the mean
The total area under the curve equals 1 (or 100%)
Standard Deviation determines the width of the bell
Almost all data (99.7%) falls within 3 standard deviations
educational.emphasis: Visualizing the 'area' as the 'probability' or 'portion of the total'.

logic_steps: Define Eigenvectors as vectors that do not rotate during transformation
Show that scaling factor is the Eigenvalue
Demonstrate that a matrix of eigenvectors (P) transforms the system to an axis-aligned (diagonal) state
Explain that Diagonalization simplifies complex transformations into independent scalings

scenes.title: Introduction to Linear Transformations
scenes.description: Visualize a standard 2D grid transforming under a generic matrix A. Show how most vectors rotate and change direction, creating a complex distortion.

scenes.title: The Special Vectors: Eigen-stuff
scenes.description: Highlight specific vectors that stay on their original span (line) during the transformation. Introduce the equation Av = λv. Show λ as the scaling factor.

scenes.title: Geometric Intuition of Diagonalization
scenes.description: Show the basis change. Rotate the coordinate system to align with the eigenvectors. In this new view, the matrix A becomes a diagonal matrix D (simple scaling along axes).
visual_elements: Transition from skewed grid to rectangular grid

scenes.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
scenes.description: Recap that Diagonalization is finding the 'natural axes' of a transformation. Reiterate A=PDP^{-1}.

key_points: Eigenvectors represent the 'principal axes' of a transformation
Diagonalization is a change of basis to simplify matrix operations
Geometrically, it turns a 'shear/rotation' mix into pure 'scaling'
educational.emphasis: Focus on the geometry of the grid changing and the stability of the eigenvector lines, rather than just the algebraic calculation.
